subject: Culture
title: Cotton and Colonialism
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Cotton and Colonialism.

hook.text: India produced the world's finest cotton for centuries. Britain destroyed the industry to sell machine-made fabric back.

buildup.text: Bengal muslin was so fine it was called 'woven air.' British tariffs and bans crushed Indian textile exports.

discovery.text: American cotton plantations relied on enslaved labor. The fabric of everyday life was woven with human suffering.

twist.text: Gandhi's spinning wheel wasn't just a symbol. Making your own cloth was an act of economic warfare against Britain.

climax.text: Today Bangladesh exports $35 billion in garments annually. Colonial patterns restructured but didn't disappear.

punchline.text: Every T-shirt has a political history.

quiz.question: What was Bengal muslin nicknamed for its fineness?

details.summary: Cotton's history is inseparable from colonialism and slavery. Britain destroyed India's cotton industry to feed its own mills, while enslaved Africans picked cotton that built American wealth. The fabric in your clothes carries centuries of exploitation and empire.
details.whyItMatters: Cotton's colonial history shows how a simple commodity shaped global power relations. Understanding this past is essential for confronting modern textile industry exploitation.
takeaways: Britain deliberately dismantled India's superior cotton industry
American slavery was driven by cotton's economic value
Cotton remains the world's most widely used natural fiber

faq.question: How did Britain destroy India's cotton industry?
faq.answer: Britain imposed tariffs on Indian textiles, flooded Indian markets with cheap machine-made cloth, and broke the fingers of skilled Indian weavers according to some accounts. India went from being the world's largest textile exporter to a raw cotton supplier for British mills within decades.

faq.question: How central was cotton to American slavery?
faq.answer: Cotton was the engine of American slavery. By 1860, cotton accounted for over 60% of US exports. The invention of the cotton gin in 1793 made cotton enormously profitable, dramatically increasing demand for enslaved labor. Four million enslaved people worked primarily in cotton by the Civil War.
